title: PDCAT: Preference-Driven Compiler Auto-Tuning
task_title: Efficient Compiler Auto-Tuning for Optimization Flag Selection

sections.title: PDCAT: Preference-Driven Compiler Auto-tuning
sections.text:
MINGXUAN ZHU, Peking University, China

ZEYU SUN, Institute of Software at Chinese Academy of Sciences, China DAN HAO<sup>∗</sup>, Peking University, China

Compilers are crucial software tools that usually convert programs in high-level languages into machine code. A compiler provides hundreds of optimizations to improve the performance of the compiled code, which are controlled by enabled or disabled optimization flags. However, the vast number of combinations of these flags makes it extremely challenging to select the desired settings for compiler optimization flags (i.e., an optimization sequence) for a given target program. In the literature, many auto-tuning techniques have been proposed to select a desired optimization sequence via diferent strategies across the entire optimization space. However, due to the huge optimization space, these techniques commonly sufer from the widely recognized eficiency problem. To address this problem, in this paper, we propose a preference-driven selection approach PDCAT, which reduces the search space of optimization sequences through three components. In particular, PDCAT first identifies combined optimizations based on compiler documentation to exclude optimization sequences violating the combined constraints, and then categorizes the optimizations into a common optimization set (whose optimization flags are fixed) and an exploration set containing the remaining optimizations. Finally, within the search process, PDCAT assigns distinct enable probabilities to the explored optimization flags and finally selects a desired optimization sequence. The former two components reduce the search space by removing invalid optimization sequences and fixing some optimization flags, whereas the latter performs a biased search in the search space. To evaluate the performance of the proposed approach PDCAT, we conducted an extensive experimental study on the latest version of the GCC compiler with two widely used benchmarks, cBench and PolyBench. The results show that PDCAT significantly outperforms the four compared techniques, including the state-of-art technique SRTuner. Moreover, each component of PDCAT not only contributes to its performance, but also improves the acceleration performance of the compared techniques.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
Compilers play an important role in software development [10–12]. They usually transform programs written in high-level languages into executable machine code. During this compilation process, compiler optimizations can be applied to achieve various objectives, e.g., reducing the size

of compiled code or improving the runtime performance of compiled code. Although GCC provides default optimization settings, such as -O1, -O2, and -O3, these default settings do not often perform well, possibly resulting in larger compiled code or worse runtime performance. Therefore, it is crucial to give a specific compiler optimization setting for a program, particularly for programs that run frequently and whose execution is time-consuming, e.g., Blender, Autodesk Maya, etc. This problem is called the compiler-tuning problem in the literature [1, 2, 13, 17, 22, 25, 33, 39, 40]. Compiler tuning involves selecting suitable compiler optimizations (i.e., referred to as “flag selection” or “phase selection”) and deciding the order in which these optimizations should be applied (i.e., referred to as “phase ordering”) [39]. As the latter phase does not apply to most compilers (e.g., GCC), this paper focuses on the former phase.

Common compilers like GCC provide hundreds of optimizations, e.g., loop unrolling and dead code elimination, which are implemented by controlling specific optimization flags (e.g., -floopunroll-and-jam, -fdce, etc.) enabled or disabled. Enabling an optimization flag does not always improve the runtime performance of a program. Due to the large number of optimizations and their exponential combinations, it is dificult for compiler users to understand the impact of each compiler flag on the target program and manually choose compiler optimization flag combinations (i.e., referred to as optimization sequences) for the program. To reduce human efort in setting compiler optimizations, numerous auto-tuning techniques [1, 2, 13, 17, 22, 25, 33, 39, 40] specifically focusing on flag selection have been proposed in the literature.

The existing auto-tuning techniques regard flag selection as a searching problem, i.e., the combinations of optimization flags compose an optimization space and compiler auto-tuning aims to explore this optimization space through some searching strategy. Following this intuition, various searching strategies, e.g., hill-climbing-based algorithm [2] and genetic algorithm [17, 19, 26, 37], have been proposed, to select a desired optimization sequence. During the searching process, these techniques usually generate numerous optimization sequences, whose corresponding runtime performance of the target program is assessed through compilation and execution. Besides these fixed search strategies, recently some researchers [15, 27, 28, 33] attempted to apply reinforcement learning in the search process, which dynamically adjusts selection strategies during the search process by the rewards calculated based on the runtime performance of existing selected optimization sequences. To sum up, the existing compiler auto-tuning techniques can be characterized by their various search strategies but share the same optimization space. The entire optimization space is huge, and thus exploration in the optimization space tends to be very time-consuming, resulting in unsatisfactory optimization sequences. Therefore, narrowing the optimization space may be a promising direction for compiler auto-tuning because of the reduced searching space.

To narrow the optimization space in compiler auto-tuning, we identify three types ofoptimization preference based on our understanding: (1) combined optimizations, which refers to the set of optimizations that are expected to be used together following the documentation of a compiler; (2) diverse optimizations, which mean that for any program enabling diferent optimizations may result in decreased or increased runtime performance; (3) common optimizations, which refers to the set of optimizations whose default setting is given by the compiler. Based on combined optimizations and common optimizations, we remove invalid optimization sequences and ignore the combination among common optimizations, resulting in a reduced optimization space. With our identification of diverse optimization, our search for the desired optimization sequences starts from the optimization sequences whose individual optimization flags have various (not equal) enabling probabilities, resulting in a reduced search space.

In this paper, based on these optimization preferences, we propose a preference-driven compiler auto-tuning technique, PDCAT, which first identifies combined optimizations based on compiler documentation, and categorizes the optimizations into two sets, i.e., a set of common optimizations given by the default optimization setting (e.g., -O1) of a compiler and a set composing the remaining optimizations. Then PDCAT explores the combination space of optimizations that fall in the latter set and the optimization sequences violating the combined constraints given by combined optimizations are excluded during the searching process. In particular, within this process, PDCAT first assigns to the explored optimization flags with distinct initial enable probabilities (instead of equal probabilities), which measures how likely an optimization flag is enabled, as well as presents an execution-based adjustment algorithm to modify the enable probabilities of explored flags based on the actual runtime performance for the selected optimization sequences. That is, PDCAT performs a biased search in the reduced optimization space, which is obtained via analyzing the constraints between optimization flags and setting diferent preferences for diferent flags.

To evaluate the performance of our approach, we conduct an experiment on the latest widely-used compiler GCC 13.1.0 using two widely used benchmarks cBench and PolyBench. For comparison, we select four representative techniques, including RIO [14], CFSCA [39], CompTuner [40], and state-of-the-art technique SRTuner [33]. For overall efectiveness, PDCAT achieves 5.5%-81.2% acceleration performance over GCC default -O3 optimization setting in all 28 selected cases in 5,000 seconds. Moreover, the optimization sequences generated by PDCAT are significantly better than all compared techniques. In particular, PDCAT achieves the best optimization results in 14 out of 28 cases. For ablation analysis, we construct 14 variants based on PDCAT by varying its three components, and PDCAT achieves a better average acceleration performance than all the variants, which demonstrates the impact of each component of PDCAT. Besides, the acceleration performance of compared techniques<sup>1</sup> also increases when afiliated with each component of PDCAT.

The contributions of this paper are summarized below.

• A preference-driven compiler auto-tuning technique PDCAT, which first identifies the combined optimizations and categorizes the optimizations into common and explored optimization sets, then conducts a biased search for the explored optimization flags.

• An extensive experiment on the latest version of GCC using two widely-used benchmarks cBench and PolyBench, which demonstrates the outperformance of PDCAT as well as its components.

• A reproducible package, available in a public repository [38].

sections.title: 2.1 Huge Optimization Space of Compiler Tuning
sections.text:
Compilers provide hundreds of optimization flags to control distinct optimizations that enhance either the runtime performance or the size of the compiled code. Given a compiler, its set of optimizations can be represented by $O = \{ o _ { 1 } , o _ { 2 } , . . . , o _ { n } \}$ , where � represents the number of optimizations and the value of $o _ { i }$ (where $1 \leq i \leq n )$ represents whether the corresponding optimization flag is enabled or disabled (i.e., $o _ { i }$ is set to 1 or 0). A specific setting of these optimization flags can be represented by a 0/1 sequence, called an optimization sequence. Although we focus on optimization flags whose values are only 0 or 1 following previous works, the entire optimization space—including all possible optimization sequences—is still very huge, e.g., GCC 13.1.0 has more than 100 optimizations, and the size of the optimization space is larger than $2 ^ { 1 0 0 }$

Due to the huge optimization space and diverse performance of each optimization flag, manually selecting the desired optimization sequence for a target program is highly ineficient and often impractical, and thus in this paper, we target at compiler auto-tuning to improve the runtime performance of target programs. In the literature, many compiler auto-tuning techniques [7, 13, 32, 33, 39, 40] have been proposed, but these techniques still struggle to select a desired compiler optimization sequence for a target program in a short time, because they try to search in the entire optimization space. However, due to the vastness of a compiler’s optimization space, searching throughout the entire space results in low search eficiency. That is, it is essential to reduce the optimization space.

sections.title: 2.2 Preferences when Selecting Optimization Flags
sections.text:
Due to the vastness of the compiler optimization space, it is impossible to perform in-depth exploration among all optimization flags. Depending on the diferent auxiliary information, we may allocate compiler tuning relevant preferences in the exploration process to reduce the optimization space.

Firstly, some compiler documentation records certain relationships between compiler optimizations and how the related optimization flags are recommended to be used in combination. Identifying such combined optimizations can help users select related optimization flags together, thus reducing the exploration of some optimization flags and reducing the optimization space. Secondly, enabling an optimization flag does not always improve the runtime performance of a compiled program (i.e., some flags generally improve runtime performances across most programs, while some flags may reduce target programs’ performance when enabled) [13, 33, 39]. Not treating the optimization flags equally can prevent excessive searching for the low-impact flags, thereby reducing the optimization space. Thirdly, there are common optimizations (e.g., -O1/-O2/-O3 provided by the compiler) used by compiler users. Although these optimizations are not very good for every target program, real-world experience has shown that these common optimizations can achieve some speedup performance on most programs. So avoiding over-exploration of common optimizations can drastically reduce the optimization space.

Inspired by these motivations, in this paper, we attempt to feed compiler tuning preferences in technique design, to reduce the optimization space.

sections.title: 3 Technique
sections.text:
Compiler auto-tuning is significantly challenging because a large number of optimization flags creates an extensive optimization space. Although many researchers have proposed numerous auto-tuning techniques, the optimization results are still unsatisfactory because these techniques often explore the entire optimization space without preference, typically overlooking the combined optimizations, assuming equal probabilities for enabling the optimization flags, and trying to explore all of the optimization flags.

However, not all optimization flags in the entire optimization flag set � contribute equally to program acceleration, nor are all optimization combinations worth exploring. As our identified three types of optimization preference, i.e., combined optimizations, diverse optimizations and common optimizations, we identify combined constraints given by combined optimizations through compiler documentation, and classify the entire optimization flag set � into two categories $O _ { c }$ (i.e., common optimization flag set) and $O _ { e }$ (i.e., explored optimization flag set), where $O _ { c }$ is the set of optimization flags given by the default optimization setting $( \mathbf { e . g . , - O 1 } )$ of a compiler, while $O _ { e }$ contains the remaining optimization flags that need to be explored. Instead of searching in $O ,$ in this paper, we propose a novel preference-driven compiler auto-tuning technique, PDCAT, which focuses on $O _ { e }$ and performs biased search under the guidance of combined constraints.

Fig. 1 shows the overview of PDCAT, which consists of three components: (1) combined optimization analysis, (2) initial enable probabilities acquisition, and (3) tuning on target program. In particular, the first component is to determine the combined constraints given by combined optimizations based on compiler documentation, the second component is to assign an initial enable probability to each flag in the explored flag set $O _ { e }$ , so that to enable optimization flags based on diferent enable probabilities, whereas the final component is to find a desired optimization sequence for the target program through a biased search under combined constraints.

![](images/c947c71f28c46c6f5ab7b35cb9e5fa80defbdae75c96e16a0c507a33fbf1ee0d.jpg)  
Fig. 1. Workflow of PDCAT.

• Combined optimization analysis determines the combined constraints ofdiferent optimization flags through the compiler documentation, so that to avoid generating optimization sequences that violate constraints and improve tuning eficiency. More details are provided in Section 3.1.

• Initial enable probabilities acquisition assigns initial enable probabilities to the flags in $O _ { e }$ through the probability distribution derived from the performance data ofthe well-performing generated optimization sequences under combined constraints on selected programs using a Bayesian model. More details are provided in Section 3.2.

• Tuning on target program finds a desired optimization sequence through a biased search under combined constraints. In particular, PDCAT randomly enables flags in $O _ { e }$ based on the enable probabilities and generates complete optimization sequences with the common flags in $O _ { c }$ under constraints. Moreover, PDCAT dynamically adjusts the enable probabilities of the flags in $O _ { e }$ based on the actual runtime performance for the selected optimization sequences. More details are provided in Section 3.3.

sections.title: 3.1 Combined Optimizations Analysis
sections.text:
Due to the combined efects between some optimizations, PDCAT attempts to analyze the combination optimizations through the compiler documentation, so that to obtain the combined constraints and avoid constraint-violating optimization sequences generated during the search process, thereby reducing the optimization space and improving the search eficiency. In detail, combined optimizations may have interactions, e.g., optimization flag -forward-propagate and optimization flag -floop-unroll-and-jam. If we disable flag -floop-unroll-and-jam, enabling -forward-propagate will be considered inefective due to the dependency constraints2. Table 1. Descriptions of combined constraints

Many compilers have documentation recording their optimization flags, including the potential combined relationships and mutual influences between diferent optimization flags. Here we use the GCC online documentation [36] as an example to introduce the constraints analysis of PDCAT. According to GCC’s online documentation, GCC’s combined optimizations can be classified into three categories according to the flags’ descriptions. • Strong dependency. When a flag is disabled, flags that strongly depend on it will have no efect. When generating optimization sequences, PDCAT checks for flags with strong dependencies to ensure that scenarios where a depended-upon flag is disabled while a flag that strongly depends on it is enabled do not occur. • Weak dependency. When a flag is enabled, flags that weakly depend on it will also be enabled. When generating optimization sequences, PDCAT ensures that when a weakly dependedupon flag is enabled, the flags that weakly depend on it are also enabled. Otherwise, if the weakly depended-upon flag is disabled, the flags that depend on it can be freely enabled or disabled. • Synergistic relationship. Two flags with a synergistic relationship will be efective when enabled together. When generating optimization sequences, PDCAT ensures that flags with a synergistic relationship are enabled together. Following these combined optimizations, we summarize three types of combined constraints. Table 1 presents the part of the combined constraints classification table, where the first column presents the combined constraints, the second column presents the categories of the corresponding combined optimizations, and the last column presents some examples. In total, we have collect 5 strong dependency constraints, 10 weak dependency constraints, and 1 synergistic relationship constraints, excluding over $2 ^ { 1 0 }$ optimization sequences3. Due to space limitations, we present the complete classification table on our website [38].

sections.title: 3.2 Initial Enable Probabilities Acquisition
sections.text:
In this component, PDCAT utilizes a Bayesian Model [3, 23] to analyze the probability distribution of these flags based on historical data from well-performing optimization sequences (i.e., acceleration performance outperforms -O3 optimization setting) across various programs. Diferent optimization flags can have distinct efects on program performance. Therefore, the propensity to enable these flags should diverse accordingly, and the likelihood of their enabling can be finely controlled through the calculated enable probabilities. Compared to treating all explored flags equally, this approach can reduce the optimization space.

In order to obtain the initial enable probabilities $P r o _ { i n i }$ of the flags in the explored optimization flag set $O _ { e }$ , we first randomly generate optimization sequences under combined constraints and obtain their performance on the selected initial tuning program set $P ,$ and then build a probability distribution model to obtain these flags’ probabilities distribution through the selected data.

Specifically, within the entire program set<sup>4</sup>, PDCAT randomly divides it into initial tuning program set � and testing program set $T$ at a ratio. For each program $\mathbf { \nabla } \mathcal { P } i$ in the initial tuning program set $P ,$ PDCAT randomly generates a fixed number of optimization sequences $S _ { i } .$ However, to avoid the increased execution time due to generating inefective optimization sequences, PDCAT checks if the generated sequences violate the combined constraints described in Section 3.1. If a violation occurs, PDCAT continuously regenerates new sequences until a compliant one is produced. Subsequently, PDCAT compiles and executes each program $\mathbf { \nabla } \mathcal { P } i$ using the corresponding generated optimization sequences, recording their runtime performance. As we hope that enabling optimization flags will result in better acceleration, optimization sequences that perform well are more valuable in observing the efects of flags in the explored optimization flag set $O _ { e }$ . Therefore, PDCAT selects the well-performing optimization sequences as dataset $D ,$ whose runtime performances outperform the compiler default -O3 optimization setting. PDCAT uses these selected sequences to analyze the probability distribution of flags in the explored optimization flag set $O _ { e }$

$$
P ( o _ { i } | D ) = \frac { \alpha + N ( o _ { i } ) } { \alpha + \beta + | D | }\tag{1}
$$

Due to Bayesian model’s ability to efectively learn by integrating prior knowledge with new data [3, 18, 23, 29]. PDCAT employs a Bayesian Model as Formula 1, where $P ( o _ { i } | D )$ is the posterior probability of flag $o _ { i }$ given the dataset $D , N ( o _ { i } )$ is number of sequences where flag $o _ { i }$ is set to 1, |�| is the size of the dataset $D ,$ � and $\beta$ are the hyper-parameters of the Beta distribution<sup>5</sup>, using the better-performing sequences as input, to determine the probability distribution of these flags, which are used as the initial enable probabilities $P r o _ { i n i }$ for the flags in $O _ { e }$

sections.title: 3.3 Tuning on Target Program
sections.text:
Tuning on a target program involves adjusting the initial enable probabilities to select a desired optimization sequence for a new target program. Since optimization flags impact diferent programs uniquely, the initial enable probabilities of the optimization flags in $O _ { e }$ , obtained from existing tuning data, require further adjustments based on the specific optimization outcomes observed on the target program.

To achieve this, we propose an execution-based adjustment algorithm that repeats optimization sequence generation by a biased search in $O _ { e }$ . For each iteration, PDCAT firstly generates the two sequences separately and combines them to compose one optimization sequence. An optimization sequence can be represented by an array $S = [ s _ { 1 } , s _ { 2 } , \ldots , s _ { m } , s _ { m + 1 } , \ldots , s _ { n } ]$ , where $s _ { 1 } - s _ { m }$ denotes whether the corresponding optimization flag $o _ { i }$ in the explored optimization flag set $O _ { e }$ is enabled or disabled (i.e., 1 or 0) while $s _ { m + 1 } - s _ { n }$ denotes the flags in the common optimization flag set $O _ { c }$ . In particular, PDCAT randomly enables the flags in $O _ { e }$ based the enable probabilities (in particular, for the first iteration, we use initial enable probabilities from the second component of PDCAT), resulting in a sequence. Then, PDCAT combines the sequence with the common sequence composed of the flags in $O _ { c }$ that given by the default -O1 optimization setting of GCC compiler<sup>6</sup>. Moreover,

PDCAT checks whether the generated sequence violates the combined constraints; if it does, PDCAT regenerates new sequences until a compliant one is produced.

Using the generated sequence, the proposed execution-based adjustment algorithm dynamically adjusts the enable probabilities of explored optimization flags based on the actual execution runtime performance $( \mathrm { i . e . , }$ acceleration performance over -O3 optimization setting) of them on the target program. The execution-based tuning algorithm calculates the efectiveness of the generated sequence as Formula 2:

$$
E _ { t } = \frac { p e r _ { t } - p e r _ { m i n } } { p e r _ { m a x } - p e r _ { m i n } }\tag{2}
$$

where $E _ { t }$ is efectiveness of sequence generated under enable probabilities $P _ { t - 1 }$ in the $t _ { t h }$ iteration (in particular, for the first iteration, we use initial enable probabilities from the second component of PDCAT), $\mathit { p e r } _ { t }$ is the runtime performance of sequence generated under enable probabilities $P _ { t - 1 }$ in the $t _ { t h }$ iteration, $p e r _ { m a x }$ represents the highest runtime performance observed among the generated sequences, while $p e r _ { m i n }$ represents the lowest.

A higher efectiveness $E _ { t }$ indicates that the optimization sequence generated with $P _ { t - 1 }$ performs better. Based on the efectiveness, PDCAT updates the enable probabilities of flags in $O _ { e }$ . If enabling a flag results in an efectiveness increasing (i.e., the efectiveness exceeds the average efectiveness), or disabling a flag results in a efectiveness decreasing (i.e., the efectiveness is below the average efectiveness), it indicates that enabling this flag leads to better performance improvement. Therefore, the enable probability of this flag increases. Conversely, the enable probability of this flag decreases. That is, PDCAT updates the enable probabilities as in Formula 3, which is widely used in dynamic adjustment strategies [21].

$$
\begin{array} { r } { P _ { t } = \left\{ \begin{array} { l l } { P _ { t - 1 } + \lambda \cdot | E _ { t } - \overline { { E } } | \cdot \left( 1 - P _ { t - 1 } \right) } & { { \mathrm { i f } } E _ { t } \geq \overline { { E } } , } \\ { P _ { t - 1 } - \lambda \cdot | E _ { t } - \overline { { E } } | \cdot P _ { t - 1 } } & { { \mathrm { i f } } E _ { t } < \overline { { E } } . } \end{array} \right. } \end{array}\tag{3}
$$

where $P _ { t }$ is the enable probabilities obtained from the update in the $t _ { t h }$ iteration, $P _ { t - 1 }$ is the enable probabilities of the $( t - 1 ) _ { t h }$ iteration (in particular, for the first iteration, we use initial enable probabilities from the second component of PDCAT), $E _ { t }$ is efectiveness of optimization sequence generated under enable probabilities $P _ { t - 1 }$ in the $t _ { t h }$ iteration $( P _ { 0 } = P r o _ { i n i } )$ , � is the average efectiveness of all � values from 1 to � iterations, and � is the scaling factor.

At the end of each iteration, PDCAT obtains new enable probabilities $P _ { t }$ for the explored optimization flags for subsequent iteration and records the optimization sequence $O _ { b e s t }$ with the highest runtime performance. Specifically, if the runtime performance of the sequence generated in the current iteration exceeds the previous best performance, then PDCAT updates $O _ { b e s t }$ . If not, PDCAT maintains $O _ { b e s t }$ unchanged.

Ultimately, reaching the termination $( \mathrm { i . e . } _ { \cdot }$ , 5,000s in our setting), PDCAT obtains the desired optimization sequence $O _ { b e s t }$ , which has the highest runtime performance during the tuning process.

sections.title: 4 Experiment Setup
sections.text:
To evaluate the performance of PDCAT, this experiment is designed to answer two research questions.

• RQ1: Efectiveness. How does PDCAT perform compared to the state-of-the-art compiler auto-tuning techniques? This RQ investigates the performance of optimization sequences selected by compiler auto-tuning techniques.

• RQ2: Ablation analysis. How does each component of PDCAT contribute to the performance? This RQ investigates the impact of each component in PDCAT.

sections.title: 4.1 Dataset
sections.text: In this experiment, we employ the latest C compiler GCC 13.1.0 as the target compiler. As the existing works [13, 39, 40], we use the widely used benchmarks cBench [9] and PolyBench [35] as target programs<sup>7</sup>, which cover a wide range of practical functions ranging from 100 to 26,000 lines of code. Table 2 presents the detailed statistics of the target programs, where the “ID” column with C1-C28 denotes the identifiers for the 28 programs from cBench, and P1-P30 denotes the identifiers for the 30 programs from PolyBench.

sections.title: 4.2 Compared Techniques
sections.text:
To validate the efectiveness of our technique, we compare it against four representative baselines: (1) RIO [14], which is a random iterative optimization technique and is usually taken as a baseline in the existing works [13, 39, 40], (2) CFSCA [39], which identifies critical optimization flags to speedup the searching process, (3) CompTuner [40], which selects an optimization sequence through multiple-phase learning, and (4) SRTuner [33], which selects an optimization sequence through an interaction process. In particular, CFSCA, CompTuner, and SRTuner are the latest published compiler auto-tuning techniques. SRTuner is the state-of-the-art compiler auto-tuning technique, which has achieved the best auto-tuning performance so far.

For a fair comparison, we set a time budget as the termination condition of the compared techniques and compare the optimization sequences generated by these techniques. In particular, we set the time budget to be 1,250, 2,500, and 5,000 seconds, respectively, so as to investigate its influence. Moreover, we repeat each technique five times to alleviate the influence of randomness resulting from the compiler auto-tuning techniques and use the median result to denote the performance of an auto-tuning technique.

sections.title: 4.3 Implementation
sections.text:
We implement PDCAT in Python based on numpy [31]. In particular, in implementing the acquisition of initial enable probabilities of PDCAT, we select 70% of the total programs (i.e., C1-C28 and P1- P30), which amounts to 40 programs, to serve as the initial tuning set<sup>8</sup>. We collect the optimization sequences’ performances on these selected programs. To minimize the influence of randomness, we conduct three separate random selections of the initial tuning set and compare the acceleration efects on the remaining test programs after each selection. For each initial tuning program, we randomly generate 500 optimization sequences, balancing data diversity and execution time. In implementing the execution-based tuning algorithm of PDCAT , we set � to 0.5, so that to maintain a balance between exploration and exploitation.

In implementing the compared techniques, we directly use their code if they provide a reproducible package (i.e., for CFSCA, CompTuner and SRTuner); otherwise, we re-implement the technique (i.e., RIO) strictly following the description in the paper. The experiment is performed on a workstation with Intel Xeon CPU E5-2680 v4@2.40GHz with 251G memory and Ubuntu 18.04.6 LTS operating system.

This process yields two compiled programs $P _ { s }$ and $P _ { d }$ . sections.title: 5.1 Overall Efectiveness (RQ1)
sections.text:
To answer RQ1, we evaluate the performance of various compiler auto-tuning techniques against the standard -O3 optimization setting. We analyze the speedup ratios across multiple iterations and target programs, highlighting the most and least efective techniques. Table 3 presents the acceleration performances of optimization sequences produced by the compared techniques. Each cell in the table indicates the speedup ratio over -O3 setting, with higher values signifying more efective auto-tuning. For each target program, the best result is highlighted in bold, while the worst is underlined. Due to the iterative selection of diferent target programs, some are tested multiple times. Thus, for programs selected more than once, Table 3 includes the average acceleration performance across these selections and notes the frequency of each program’s selection. From this table, the acceleration performance of PDCAT varies from 5.1% to 81.2% in 5,000 seconds, indicating that the optimization sequences generated by PDCAT are better than the default -O3 optimization on all target programs. Furthermore, as the time budget increases from 1,250 seconds to 5,000 seconds, the performance of PDCAT presents a corresponding increase. 5.1.1 Statistics Analysis. To further investigate whether PDCAT outperforms the compared baselines, we statistically analyze the experimental results from four perspectives. Firstly, we observe in how many cases where the compared techniques perform worse than PDCAT in diferent time budgets. Secondly, we explore the best technique by analyzing how many cases a technique achieves the best optimization result and the worst result. Thirdly, we compare the overall acceleration performance of diferent techniques by analyzing the average acceleration performance for all cases in 5,000 seconds. Finally, we perform significant analysis on PDCAT and other techniques. sections.title: 5.2.3 Combined Optimization Analysis.
sections.text:
Withoutcombined optimization analysis. To investigate the contribution ofthe combined optimizations, we do not exclude the generated optimization sequences that violate combined constraints when tuning on target programs, resulting in a major variant of PDCAT (denoted as $P D C A T _ { N o C o m b } )$ Table 7 presents the acceleration performances of optimization sequences produced by PDCAT and $P D C A T _ { N o C o m b }$ on the selected test programs, with better results highlighted in bold. Due to the random selection, some programs, e.g., C1, C2, do not appear in the table as initial tuning programs.

We discover that PDCAT’s performance decreases without combined constraints in most cases, indicating the contribution of combined optimization analysis. From Table 7, $P D C A T _ { N o C o m b }$ achieves better acceleration performance in 5/4/5 of the 18 cases and an average acceleration performance of 15.3% in 5,000 seconds. Sometimes $P D C A T _ { N o C o m b }$ obtains better results than PDCAT, which indicates the limited impact of the combined optimization analysis. In the cases (e.g., C9, P4, etc.) where $P D C A T _ { N o C o m b }$ outperforms PDCAT, the optimization sequences generated by $P D C A T _ { N o C o m b }$ also satisfy the combined constraints. As combined optimizations involve fewer optimizations and some optimizations fall into the common optimization set (e.g., -forward-propagate), $P D C A T _ { N o C o m b }$ occasionally generate optimization sequences under the similar search processes of PDCAT that satisfy the combined constraints. That is, the limited number of combined optimizations does not significantly enhance the overall tuning efectiveness.

Combined optimization analysis for other techniques. Moreover, to verify the impact of combined optimizations on other techniques, we modify the compared techniques (i.e., CFSCA, CompTuner, and SRTuner) by adding combined constraints check during searching process, resulting in three secondary variants (denoted as $C F C S A _ { C o m b } ;$ $C o m p T u n e r _ { C o m b } ,$ and $S R T u n e r _ { C o m b } )$ $C F C S A _ { C o m b } ,$ $C o m p T u n e r _ { C o m b }$ , and $S R T u n e r _ { C o m b }$ achieve average acceleration efects of 13.9%, 13.5%, and 15.2% in 18 cases in 5,000 seconds, respectively. Although their results yet do not outperform PDCAT, there is an improvement compared to the acceleration performance of 13.7%, 13.1%, and 14.6% achieved by CFSCA, CompTuner, and SRTuner without combined constraints in 5,000 seconds. This demonstrates the efectiveness of the combined constraints we apply.

sections.title: 6 Threats to Validity
sections.text:
The internal threat mainly arises from the implementation of compiler auto-tuning approaches. To reduce this threat, we utilize the reproducible packages of the compared approaches and strictly re-implement these approaches based on their corresponding publications when reproducible packages are unavailable. Besides, the authors review the implementations to further reduce this threat.

The external threat mainly comes from the target programs, compilers and target platforms. To reduce this threat, we use the same benchmarks, the latest version of a popular compiler and most commonly x86 platform as previous work did.

The construct threat in our evaluation comes from the used metrics. GCC provides several optimization settings, including -O1, -O2, -O3, and -Ofast. Notably, -Ofast extends -O3 by incorporating some unconventional optimizations that may violate certain international standards. In contrast, -O1 and -O2 do not activate many optimization flags. Consequently, -Ofast is generally not recommended in the literature, and studies on compiler tuning are typically compared against -O3. Following previous works [13, 33, 39, 40], we also use the acceleration performance over the compiler’s default -O3 optimization.

sections.title: 7 Discussion
sections.text: In this section, we discuss the applicability of the proposed PDCAT on other compilers, the impact of varying input data on tuning performance, and file-specific tuning for a program.

sections.title: 7.1 Applicability for Other Compilers
sections.text: Our proposed approach, PDCAT, is also applicable to auto-tuning for other compilers $( \mathrm { e . g . , L L V M } ) .$ PDCAT treats a compiler’s optimization flags as selection targets and follows a three-step process. For diferent compilers, the first step of PDCAT, combined optimizations analysis, focuses on analyzing combined optimizations to reduce the optimization space. Although some compilers may not provide detailed oficial documentation specifying combined optimizations which PDCAT relies on, certain constraints are represented in the compiler’s source code. These constraints can serve as a supplementary source for identifying valid combined optimizations. Meanwhile, the second step, initial enable probabilities acquisition, and the third step, tuning on target program, can be directly applied to any compiler without modification. Thus, adapting PDCAT for diferent compilers only requires adjusting the input optimization flags and identifying their combined constraints, ensuring the applicability of PDCAT across various compilers.

sections.title: 7.2 Impact of Input Data Variability
sections.text: Among the two selected benchmarks, PolyBench uses fixed inputs, whereas cBench allows diferent input data, which can be specified as parameters. In our experiments, we used the default inputs of cBench to ensure consistency in comparison. Variations in input size, complexity, and boundary conditions influence execution time. Since the tuning process relies on execution time as feedback, longer runtimes result in fewer iterations when the tuning time is fixed. Additionally, diferent inputs can trigger distinct program behaviors (e.g., variations in loops or branches), necessitating diferent optimization strategies. Our proposed approach, PDCAT, selects from a comprehensive set of optimization flags, covering optimizations for diverse code structures, thereby enabling efective tuning across diferent inputs.

sections.title: 7.3 File-Specific Tuning
sections.text: For multi-file projects, current compiler auto-tuning techniques [14, 33, 39, 40], including our proposed PDCAT, treat the entire project as the tuning target and select an desired compiler optimization sequence to improve the project’s runtime performance. In multi-file projects, each source file may have distinct characteristics, requiring diferent optimization strategies to achieve the best performance. File-specific tuning presents a promising direction for compiler auto-tuning. By tuning each file individually, it is possible to tailor the optimization process to the specific needs of diferent code, potentially leading to more eficient execution. While this approach may increase the overall tuning time due to the added complexity of per-file optimization, it can also result in significant performance improvements by allowing finer-grained control over the applied optimizations. Future research could explore strategies to balance tuning eficiency and performance gains.

sections.title: 8 Related Work
sections.text:
Tuning is a critical problem in both engineering and research domains. Many systems and models provide a very large number of configurable parameters, which require fine-tuning to meet diverse demands. This paper specifically focuses on compiler auto-tuning, thus is most related to compiler auto-tuning. Therefore, in this section, we will provide a detailed review of existing work on compiler auto-tuning.

Compiler auto-tuning focuses on recommending optimization settings to enhance program runtime performance, which typically involves selecting optimization flags and determining their application order, known as phase ordering. For instance, Ashouri et al. [5] clusters LLVM’s optimization flags to create sub-optimization sequences, builds a pre-train prediction model by these sub-optimization sequences, and uses the pre-train model to predict a desired application order of optimization flags. Similarly, Huang et al. [20] proposed a reinforcement learning-based technique that predicts the appropriate optimization flag order based on the program’s characteristics and previously used flags. Kulkarni et al. [24] first applied deep reinforcement learning to optimize phase ordering in JIT compilers, which utilizes dynamic program characteristics as inputs and used an augmented topology neural evolution algorithm to build neural networks.

As this paper focuses on flag selection instead ofphase ordering, we review the existing techniques which use diferent searching strategies to find a desired optimization sequence in the compiler optimization space. Chen et al. [14] proposed a random iterative optimization technique, which aims to generate a desired optimization sequence by randomly generating new sequences. To trace the searching process, some techniques (e.g., hill-climbing-based techniques [2] and genetic algorithm based techniques [17, 19, 26]) were proposed to guide compiler auto-tuning through evolutionary process. Perez et al. [34] proposed Irace, which generates optimization sequences based on historical performance distributions. OpenTuner [4] serves as a framework that integrates diferent search algorithms and allocates the most efective methods based on historical performance data. Ashouri et al. [8] proposed a Bayesian network based technique, which generates new optimization sequences through a Bayesian process. Ashouri et al. [6] also proposed Cobayn, which employs Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Exploratory Factor Analysis to reduce flags’ dimensionality and trains on program features and compiler optimization flags by Bayesian model, so that to infer the desired optimization sequences for new programs based on their features. Chen et al. [13] proposed another Bayesian network based technique BOCA, which builds a prediction model to distinguish impactful flags and performs a biased search of the impactful flags. Zhu et al. [40] proposed CompTuner, which builds a more accurate Bayesian model and then employs an intelligent search algorithm for finding desired optimization sequences. Additionally, Zhu et al. [39] proposed CFCSA, which identifies critical flags by the relationship between the functionalities of optimization flags and program structures, so that to enhance optimization eficiency through biased search of critical flags.

Reinforcement learning is increasingly used in compiler auto-tuning for its ability to continuously iterate and enhance itself [15, 27, 28]. Facebook proposed CompilerGym [16], which is a reinforcement learning environment for executing compiler optimization tasks. The current state-of-the-art technique SRTuner was developed by Park et al. [33]. Instead of selecting all optimization flags at once, SRTuner employs a multi-stage tuning strategy that tests the efects of enabling and disabling diferent flags on program performance and make selection after comparing the results.

sections.title: 9 Conclusion
sections.text: To alleviate human eforts on compiler tuning for a specific program, several compiler auto-tuning techniques have been proposed in the literature, but all sufer from performance issues. In this paper, we propose PDCAT, a preference-driven compiler auto-tuning technique. In particular, PDCAT identifies combined optimizations by compiler documentation, and categorizes the flags into common and explored optimization sets, assigning distinct enable probabilities to the explored flags for biased search. According to the experimental results on GCC and LLVM, the proposed PDCAT achieves the best runtime performances on most target programs, significantly outperforming the state-of-the-art compiler auto-tuning technique. Moreover, the ablation analysis also demonstrates the contribution of each component in PDCAT.

abstract: Compilers are crucial software tools that usually convert programs in high-level languages into machine code. A compiler provides hundreds of optimizations to improve the performance of the compiled code, which are controlled by enabled or disabled optimization flags. However, the vast number of combinations of these flags makes it extremely challenging to select the desired settings for compiler optimization flags (i.e., an optimization sequence) for a given target program. In the literature, many auto-tuning techniques have been proposed to select a desired optimization sequence via different strategies across the entire optimization space. However, due to the huge optimization space, these techniques commonly suffer from the widely recognized efficiency problem. To address this problem, in this paper, we propose a preference-driven selection approach PDCAT, which reduces the search space of optimization sequences through three components. In particular, PDCAT first identifies combined optimizations based on compiler documentation to exclude optimization sequences violating the combined constraints, and then categorizes the optimizations into a common optimization set (whose optimization flags are fixed) and an exploration set containing the remaining optimizations. Finally, within the search process, PDCAT assigns distinct enable probabilities to the explored optimization flags and finally selects a desired optimization sequence. The former two components reduce the search space by removing invalid optimization sequences and fixing some optimization flags, whereas the latter performs a biased search in the search space. To evaluate the performance of the proposed approach PDCAT, we conducted an extensive experimental study on the latest version of the GCC compiler with two widely used benchmarks, cBench and PolyBench. The results show that PDCAT significantly outperforms the four compared techniques, including the state-of-art technique SRTuner. Moreover, each component of PDCAT not only contributes to its performance, but also improves the acceleration performance of the compared techniques.
introduction:
Compilers play an important role in software development [10–12]. They usually transform programs written in high-level languages into executable machine code. During this compilation process, compiler optimizations can be applied to achieve various objectives, e.g., reducing the size

of compiled code or improving the runtime performance of compiled code. Although GCC provides default optimization settings, such as -O1, -O2, and -O3, these default settings do not often perform well, possibly resulting in larger compiled code or worse runtime performance. Therefore, it is crucial to give a specific compiler optimization setting for a program, particularly for programs that run frequently and whose execution is time-consuming, e.g., Blender, Autodesk Maya, etc. This problem is called the compiler-tuning problem in the literature [1, 2, 13, 17, 22, 25, 33, 39, 40]. Compiler tuning involves selecting suitable compiler optimizations (i.e., referred to as “flag selection” or “phase selection”) and deciding the order in which these optimizations should be applied (i.e., referred to as “phase ordering”) [39]. As the latter phase does not apply to most compilers (e.g., GCC), this paper focuses on the former phase.

Common compilers like GCC provide hundreds of optimizations, e.g., loop unrolling and dead code elimination, which are implemented by controlling specific optimization flags (e.g., -floopunroll-and-jam, -fdce, etc.) enabled or disabled. Enabling an optimization flag does not always improve the runtime performance of a program. Due to the large number of optimizations and their exponential combinations, it is dificult for compiler users to understand the impact of each compiler flag on the target program and manually choose compiler optimization flag combinations (i.e., referred to as optimization sequences) for the program. To reduce human efort in setting compiler optimizations, numerous auto-tuning techniques [1, 2, 13, 17, 22, 25, 33, 39, 40] specifically focusing on flag selection have been proposed in the literature.

The existing auto-tuning techniques regard flag selection as a searching problem, i.e., the combinations of optimization flags compose an optimization space and compiler auto-tuning aims to explore this optimization space through some searching strategy. Following this intuition, various searching strategies, e.g., hill-climbing-based algorithm [2] and genetic algorithm [17, 19, 26, 37], have been proposed, to select a desired optimization sequence. During the searching process, these techniques usually generate numerous optimization sequences, whose corresponding runtime performance of the target program is assessed through compilation and execution. Besides these fixed search strategies, recently some researchers [15, 27, 28, 33] attempted to apply reinforcement learning in the search process, which dynamically adjusts selection strategies during the search process by the rewards calculated based on the runtime performance of existing selected optimization sequences. To sum up, the existing compiler auto-tuning techniques can be characterized by their various search strategies but share the same optimization space. The entire optimization space is huge, and thus exploration in the optimization space tends to be very time-consuming, resulting in unsatisfactory optimization sequences. Therefore, narrowing the optimization space may be a promising direction for compiler auto-tuning because of the reduced searching space.

To narrow the optimization space in compiler auto-tuning, we identify three types ofoptimization preference based on our understanding: (1) combined optimizations, which refers to the set of optimizations that are expected to be used together following the documentation of a compiler; (2) diverse optimizations, which mean that for any program enabling diferent optimizations may result in decreased or increased runtime performance; (3) common optimizations, which refers to the set of optimizations whose default setting is given by the compiler. Based on combined optimizations and common optimizations, we remove invalid optimization sequences and ignore the combination among common optimizations, resulting in a reduced optimization space. With our identification of diverse optimization, our search for the desired optimization sequences starts from the optimization sequences whose individual optimization flags have various (not equal) enabling probabilities, resulting in a reduced search space.

In this paper, based on these optimization preferences, we propose a preference-driven compiler auto-tuning technique, PDCAT, which first identifies combined optimizations based on compiler documentation, and categorizes the optimizations into two sets, i.e., a set of common optimizations given by the default optimization setting (e.g., -O1) of a compiler and a set composing the remaining optimizations. Then PDCAT explores the combination space of optimizations that fall in the latter set and the optimization sequences violating the combined constraints given by combined optimizations are excluded during the searching process. In particular, within this process, PDCAT first assigns to the explored optimization flags with distinct initial enable probabilities (instead of equal probabilities), which measures how likely an optimization flag is enabled, as well as presents an execution-based adjustment algorithm to modify the enable probabilities of explored flags based on the actual runtime performance for the selected optimization sequences. That is, PDCAT performs a biased search in the reduced optimization space, which is obtained via analyzing the constraints between optimization flags and setting diferent preferences for diferent flags.

To evaluate the performance of our approach, we conduct an experiment on the latest widely-used compiler GCC 13.1.0 using two widely used benchmarks cBench and PolyBench. For comparison, we select four representative techniques, including RIO [14], CFSCA [39], CompTuner [40], and state-of-the-art technique SRTuner [33]. For overall efectiveness, PDCAT achieves 5.5%-81.2% acceleration performance over GCC default -O3 optimization setting in all 28 selected cases in 5,000 seconds. Moreover, the optimization sequences generated by PDCAT are significantly better than all compared techniques. In particular, PDCAT achieves the best optimization results in 14 out of 28 cases. For ablation analysis, we construct 14 variants based on PDCAT by varying its three components, and PDCAT achieves a better average acceleration performance than all the variants, which demonstrates the impact of each component of PDCAT. Besides, the acceleration performance of compared techniques<sup>1</sup> also increases when afiliated with each component of PDCAT.

The contributions of this paper are summarized below.

• A preference-driven compiler auto-tuning technique PDCAT, which first identifies the combined optimizations and categorizes the optimizations into common and explored optimization sets, then conducts a biased search for the explored optimization flags.

• An extensive experiment on the latest version of GCC using two widely-used benchmarks cBench and PolyBench, which demonstrates the outperformance of PDCAT as well as its components.

• A reproducible package, available in a public repository [38].
experiment:
To evaluate the performance of PDCAT, this experiment is designed to answer two research questions. • RQ1: Efectiveness. How does PDCAT perform compared to the state-of-the-art compiler auto-tuning techniques? This RQ investigates the performance of optimization sequences selected by compiler auto-tuning techniques. • RQ2: Ablation analysis. How does each component of PDCAT contribute to the performance? This RQ investigates the impact of each component in PDCAT. 4.1 Dataset In this experiment, we employ the latest C compiler GCC 13.1.0 as the target compiler. As the existing works [13, 39, 40], we use the widely used benchmarks cBench [9] and PolyBench [35] as target programs7, which cover a wide range of practical functions ranging from 100 to 26,000 lines of code. Table 2 presents the detailed statistics of the target programs, where the “ID” column with C1-C28 denotes the identifiers for the 28 programs from cBench, and P1-P30 denotes the identifiers for the 30 programs from PolyBench. 4.2 Compared Techniques To validate the efectiveness of our technique, we compare it against four representative baselines: (1) RIO [14], which is a random iterative optimization technique and is usually taken as a baseline in the existing works [13, 39, 40], (2) CFSCA [39], which identifies critical optimization flags to speedup the searching process, (3) CompTuner [40], which selects an optimization sequence through multiple-phase learning, and (4) SRTuner [33], which selects an optimization sequence through an interaction process. In particular, CFSCA, CompTuner, and SRTuner are the latest published compiler auto-tuning techniques. SRTuner is the state-of-the-art compiler auto-tuning technique, which has achieved the best auto-tuning performance so far. For a fair comparison, we set a time budget as the termination condition of the compared techniques and compare the optimization sequences generated by these techniques. In particular, we set the time budget to be 1,250, 2,500, and 5,000 seconds, respectively, so as to investigate its influence. Moreover, we repeat each technique five times to alleviate the influence of randomness resulting from the compiler auto-tuning techniques and use the median result to denote the performance of an auto-tuning technique. 4.3 Implementation We implement PDCAT in Python based on numpy [31]. In particular, in implementing the acquisition of initial enable probabilities of PDCAT, we select 70% of the total programs (i.e., C1-C28 and P1- P30), which amounts to 40 programs, to serve as the initial tuning set8. We collect the optimization sequences’ performances on these selected programs. To minimize the influence of randomness, we conduct three separate random selections of the initial tuning set and compare the acceleration efects on the remaining test programs after each selection. For each initial tuning program, we randomly generate 500 optimization sequences, balancing data diversity and execution time. In implementing the execution-based tuning algorithm of PDCAT , we set � to 0.5, so that to maintain a balance between exploration and exploitation. In implementing the compared techniques, we directly use their code if they provide a reproducible package (i.e., for CFSCA, CompTuner and SRTuner); otherwise, we re-implement the technique (i.e., RIO) strictly following the description in the paper. The experiment is performed on a workstation with Intel Xeon CPU E5-2680 v4@2.40GHz with 251G memory and Ubuntu 18.04.6 LTS operating system. 4.4 Measurement As previous work did [13, 33, 39, 40], we evaluate the runtime performance improvement of a compiler auto-tuning technique by comparing it with the compiler’s default optimization settings.
